title: GPU runtime profiling: TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM, CUDA graphs
summary: Deep dive on GPU runtime profiling results for NovaCore's 70B LLM workload. Compared vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM kernels, explored cudagraphs impact, KV cache behavior, batching tradeoffs, and quantization sensitivity. Agreed to run two targeted benchmarks (fixed latency SLO and throughput) in NovaCore's VPC and for Redwood Dedicated. Next steps: exchange traces, share kernel-level flame graphs, run INT8 quantized pass and validate regen quality.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Kapoor (Redwood AE), Marco Chen (Redwood SE), Evan Ramirez (NovaCore ML Infra), Priya Singh (NovaCore SRE), Liam O'Connor (Platform)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial): deep dive on kernel selection and cudagraphs, some noise in transcription

00:00 Speaker 1 - Aisha: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh quick agenda — kernel selection, vllm vs tensorrt-llm, cudagraphs captures, kv-cache behavior, quantization experiments, and network/VPC implications. sound good?
00:22 Speaker 2 - Evan: yep thanks Aisha, excited to dig in. we ran some microbenchmarks on our side but results were a bit noisy so hoping to reconcile with your profiling.
00:38 Speaker 3 - Marco: cool, i'll start with an overview of what we instrumented. note, our runtime picks kernels based on op shapes and seq len distributions, and sometimes will swap to a different matmul kernel mid-stream — that can cause discontinuities in latency.
01:05 Marco: we captured cuda event timelines, per-layer kernel durations, and cudagraph replay times. the cudagraphs help when the control flow is static; if you have dynamic branching or variable prompt lengths the graphs need rewarm which kills the win.
01:38 Evan: our workload is a 70B transformer with lots of short prefix caching — so many of the requests are 8-64 tokens prefix plus 256 token generation. we also use a KV cache warm start pattern across requests.
02:02 Marco: ok that explains some of the patterns. when we profiled with vllm (we ran vllm with the latest patches) we saw lower median latency for small batches but tail got worse once the KV-cache warmed up due to per-request copying/eviction work.
02:27 Priya: sorry can you unpack the evictions bit again?
02:31 Marco: sure — vllm's in-memory KV cache representation sometimes copies or reserializes keys when you do prefix reuse across sessions; depends on the allocator. tensorRT-LLM uses a more contiguous KV layout which avoids some copies but costs more up-front memory. so tradeoff is memory vs tail latency.
03:00 Liam: is that a function of our shard layout? we run 8-way model parallelism across 4 nodes, so network shuffles matter.
03:12 Marco: yes, network joins matter. with tensorrt-llm we tend to see fewer small memcpy ops but larger, contiguous transfers which can be more efficient on NVLink. vllm had more fine-grained ops which showed up in the event timeline as lots of micro kernels.
03:45 Speaker 1 - Aisha: can you show the flame graph?
03:48 Marco: yes, i'll pull up the flame. (link shared: https://redwood-internal/benchmarks/cudagraphs-2025-08) note the big spike at block_matmul_kernel_v2 which is our chosen fp16 kernel for long seqs.
04:18 Marco: when we enable cudagraphs we see two effects: 1) reduced host-to-device kernel dispatch overhead, which improves 95ish percentile latency for steady-state; 2) less flexibility for dynamic batching, so short-lived bursty traffic can actually see worse latency if graphs are reused incorrectly.
04:45 Evan: ok interesting. on our side we saw lower latency with cudagraphs in a fully deterministic pipeline, but when we had mixed prompt lengths the latency actually increased since the graph replay had to serialize different shapes.
05:12 Marco: yup, so recommended pattern is to partition traffic by shape-distribution and use separate graph pools — small-prompt graphs and long-seq graphs. Redwood runtime supports multiple graph caches and routing policy to pick the right pool.
05:41 Priya: about kernel selection — is that automatic? can we pin kernels?
05:45 Marco: it's automatic by default, but we expose overrides. you can pin a kernel family per model version or per route. pinning helps reproducibility for quantized runs where kernel math can change accuracy.
06:10 Marco: speaking of quant, we ran INT8 calibration on our sample 70B and saw a 1.5% logprobs degradation in raw perplexity in one pass; with per-channel calibration and a small calibration set it dropped to ~0.8%. 4-bit quant (QLoRA style) had a bit more variance.
06:40 Evan: that's in line with our expectations — quality loss ok up to 1% but anything more we need to test with regen accuracy on critical prompts.
06:53 Marco: agreed — we typically recommend running regen tests on your core prompt suite. Redwood Optimize can automate that and surface regressions.
07:10 Aisha: can you describe your VPC topology? any egress restrictions?
07:17 Evan: we have strict egress — peered VPC with limited NAT; we prefer Redwood Dedicated in a peered VPC to avoid public egress. also interested in private on-prem later.
07:35 Marco: good to know. for VPC setups we can provide an AMI/container for on-prem or a private control plane. network-wise, NVLink within node is fine but cross-node shuffles need careful NIC tuning — 100Gb tends to be fine but you must tune GPUDirect RDMA or use NCCL over TCP if RDMA isn't enabled.
08:05 Priya: any gotchas with cudagraphs + RDMA?
08:09 Marco: mostly about page-locked buffers; cudagraphs can capture operations that assume page-locked host pointers. If your network stack copies from pageable memory during RDMA, you can see regressions. we recommend testing with page-locked allocations when using cudagraphs across nodes.
08:40 Evan: can you comment on kernel selection differences between TensorRT-LLM and vllm concrete examples?
08:46 Marco: sure — TensorRT-LLM tends to favor large-tile matmul kernels optimized for Tensor Cores and fused attention kernels; they also have custom fused rotary/softmax ops that reduce memory traffic. vllm relies on many smaller CUDA kernels and more host orchestration, which can be great for small-batch latency but less optimal for high throughput on large seqs.
09:20 Evan: our peaks are throughput-bound during batch runs, but latency SLO is 150ms p95 for an internal route. we've been thinking Dedicated + cudagraphs to hit p95.
09:35 Marco: feasible — if you partition shapes and prewarm KV cache. Also consider dynamic batching thresholds; batching increases throughput but can push p95 up if not management carefully.
09:56 Aisha: any notes on memory fragmentation or allocator behavior?
10:01 Marco: yes, allocators matter. we saw cases where fragmentation from repeated small allocations caused OOM during long-running inference. Using a slab allocator and preallocating for KV cache reduces fragmentation. TensorRT tends to preallocate more which helps fragmentation but increases reservation. vllm's more flexible allocator trades reservation for agility.
10:35 Liam: about model sharding — anything we should change in our 8-way layout?
10:39 Marco: depends — for cudagraphs and TensorRT you want to co-locate shards to minimize cross-node communication or ensure NVLink/A2A paths; also consider reducing pipeline stages for short seqs to avoid pipeline bubbles.
11:05 Evan: do you have a suggested profiling checklist we can run to capture the same signals?
11:09 Marco: yes — we'll attach a checklist but quick version: capture cuda events + kernel names, nvprof-style timelines, host timelines for memcpy, cudagraph capture/replay logs, KV cache hit/miss counters, and end-to-end p95/p99 with and without graphs. Also collect model weights checksum and quant calibration metrics.
11:39 Priya: sounds good. any immediate red flags from the traces we sent earlier?
11:44 Marco: your traces show a repeated memcpy pattern around token 32 boundaries — looks like your batching policy is slicing prompts into micro-batches when prompts cross a threshold. that triggers multiple small kernels instead of a single longer matmul. tuning the batch combiner to avoid slicing at 32-token boundaries helped on our test.
12:10 Evan: hmm that might be from our preprocessor — we'll dig in.
12:15 Aisha: switching topics: what about autotuning and kernel selection during runtime — can we lock to avoid performance cliffs in production?
12:23 Marco: yes you can lock kernel family after a warm-up profiling run. Redwood also supports a canary mode where a small percentage of requests go through the autotuned path and we evaluate metrics before switching.
12:40 Evan: about cudagraphs again — what's the perf delta you typically see?
12:45 Marco: for steady-state long-seq workloads we saw 10-25% lower p95 latency and 15-40% higher throughput depending on kernel and hardware. but for mixed-length, small-batch workloads the win can be negative unless you partition graphs.
13:10 Liam: curious about quantization speedups vs accuracy — any numbers for INT8 on 70B?
13:16 Marco: in our experiments INT8 with tuned calibration gives roughly 1.8-2.5x throughput improvement for matmul-dominated regions, but end-to-end regen quality depends heavily on calibration. lower bit widths (4-bit) can give 3-4x gains but with more variance.
13:42 Priya: ok. how do we validate regen quality? is there tooling?
13:46 Marco: Redwood Optimize provides a regen eval harness — you feed the prompt set and we compute regeneration accuracy and delta logprobs, with per-prompt breakouts. we'll share a sample report.
14:05 Evan: excellent. one implementation detail — we use custom ops for rotary and a couple fused kernels; will those be compatible with TensorRT-LLM?
14:14 Marco: usually yes but custom ops require building TensorRT plugins; we can help with plugin development or fallback to compatible unfused kernels. building plugins gives best perf but takes extra engineering.
14:38 Speaker 2 - Evan: (inaudible)
14:45 Marco: quick note on cudagraph capture: capture needs deterministic host pointer and tensor shapes; if your preproc mutates shapes in-flight capture won't match replay. we saw a handful of user errors there.
15:10 Aisha: we've talked a lot — can we recap decisions and next steps?
15:15 Marco: recap: 1) run two benchmarks (latency SLO with cudagraphs on TRT-LLM; throughput with vllm) 2) share kernel flame graphs and capture commands 3) tune batching policy to avoid 32-token slicing 4) run INT8 calibration + regen tests on core prompt set 5) validate VPC network settings and page-locked allocation config for RDMA.
15:48 Evan: sounds good — i'll upload the traces and schedule the infra window.
15:55 Priya: we'll check peering details and send the network doc.
16:00 Aisha: i'll follow up with pricing and proposed dates for the benchmark runs.
16:05 Marco: I'll create a short profiling checklist and example cudagraph capture script and drop it in the shared drive.
16:20 Speaker 1 - Aisha: thanks everyone. end of meeting.
